children.html: Three-item loneliness scale: Exploring the psychometric properties in the Indian context
Naval Garg a , Nidhi Sharma b,* , John Burgess c
• a Delhi Technological University, New Delhi, India
• b Department of Commerce, Kirori Mal College, University of Delhi, Delhi 110007, India
Keywords: Three-item loneliness scale (TILS) Gratitude Social connectedness

The present study investigated the psychometric properties of the three-item loneliness scale (TILS) in the Indian context using two studies. Based on a sample of 570 respondents, the first study recommended the scale's factorial validity. Based on a sample of 534 respondents, the second study confirmed reliability, composite and criterion validity following rigorous statistical processes. The results suggest adequate reliability and validity of the TILS in the Indian context.

Loneliness leads to poor mental health (Suri and Garg, 2020), general anxiety (Beutel et al., 2017), depression (Yanguas et al., 2018), insomnia (Pengpid and Peltzer, 2021), psychiatric and personality disorders (Mushtaq et al., 2014), psychosis (Chau et al., 2019), paranoia (Lamster et al., 2017), dementia, Alzheimer's disease (Lee et al., 2019), and impaired cognitive functions (Pengpid and Peltzer, 2021), physical health problems (Igarashi, 2019), low energy and fatigue (Suri and Garg, 2020), obesity and diabetes (Mushtaq et al., 2014), hypertension, cardiovascular diseases (Lee et al., 2019), biological dysfunctions and physiological distress (Tiwari, 2013), poor quality of life (Musich et al., 2015), and emotional and psychological turmoil (Garg, 2020). Given its deleterious and far-reaching implications, exploring the different facets of loneliness has become imperative. It has also become crucial as loneliness has emerged as one of the fastest-growing psychosocial health concerns (Hossain et al., 2020; Saito et al., 2019) in contemporary societies like India, which is witnessing a major transition from collectivism to individualism (Hossain et al., 2020).

This undesirable transition leads to deterioration in interdependence (Clark et al., 2018), close stable relationships (Boger ¨ and Huxhold, 2018), and overall social capital (Firoz et al., 2021). There are more than 1.23 million men and 3.68 million women living alone in India (Jeyalakshmi et al., 2011). This trend has been on the rise with changes in the socio-cultural values of joint and extended families over time (Grover et al., 2019). Moreover, despite many people living in the

same house, quality interactions that could otherwise offer assurance against loneliness have also been reduced (Hossain et al., 2020). Furthermore, socioeconomic factors like low education, high poverty, accelerating dependency ratios, income inequality, rapid industrialization, unplanned urbanization, and poor transportation have increased the probability of loneliness among Indians (Tiwari, 2013). Similar sentiments voicing the ever-increasing 'loneliness crisis' have been echoed by media reports (Newmyer et al., 2021). The exponential rise in both reported and unreported cases of loneliness necessitates its exploration among Indians.

The first and foremost step in exploring a social phenomenon is the availability of a scale that allows its correct measurement, which further leads to studies on its causes, effects, and remedies. Also, given the cultural differences, it is imperative to analyze the reliability and validity of an existing scale in every culture settings. Thus, the present study investigated the psychometric properties of the three-item loneliness scale (TILS) in the Indian context. Although a few other scales, like the UCLA (University of California, Los Angeles) Loneliness scale (Russell et al., 1978), are available, modern researchers advocate smaller scales. Since response rates in social science research have been declining (Bryman, 2012), shorter scales serve as quick measures by overcoming the limitation of length that otherwise make their use difficult in larger-scale studies (Hughes et al., 2004). Thus, a three-item loneliness scale is considered in the present study. Two studies were conducted sequentially to access the reliability and validity of TILS among Indians. The first study confirmed the three-item structure of

TILS using exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). And the second study suggested adequate reliability and validity of TILS with the help of Cronbach's alpha (CA), composite reliability (CR), and average variance extracted (AVE) values.

Study 1 is based on a sample of 570 respondents, which was divided into two parts using systematic sampling. Even responses were part of subsample-1, and odd responses were included in subsample-2. Tables 1 and 2 provide details of the sampling technique, size, method of data collection, scales used and sampling description. The Cronbach's alpha values for subsample-1, subsample-2, and the overall sample were 0.826, 0.873, and 0.834. The acceptable Cronbach's alpha values are 0.70 and above. Thus, these values recommended adequate reliability of the data.

The first subsample was subjected to EFA using principal component analysis in SPSS statistics 21. The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) test and Bartlett's test of sphericity were conducted to check the factorability of the data. The KMO value of sampling adequacy was 0.910. The acceptable KMO value is 0.70 and above. Also, statistically significant Bartlett's test of sphericity was reported at a 0.05 level of significance. The findings of these tests recommended the suitability of data for EFA. EFA, conducted using varimax rotation, suggested a single-factor solution, which explains 70.20% of the total variance. Table 3 illustrates factor loadings, communalities, and total variance explained by three statements of the TILS scale. CFA was then conducted on the second subsample using analysis of moment structure (AMOS) 18. The acceptable values of different estimates are Goodness-of-fit index (GFI)≥ 0.95; Comparative-fit-index (CFI)≥ 0.97; Standardised root mean residual (SRMR)≤ 0.05; and Root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA)< 0.08 (Hu andBentler, 1999). The default model of TILS showed acceptable and consistent values, GFI= 0.970, CFI= 0.982, SRMR= 0.030, and RMSEA= 0.0461. Also, the regression weights of the three scale items were 0.764, 0.780, and 0.623, respectively. Fig. 1 reports the CFA model of the TILS. Thus, the results of EFA and CFA concluded the acceptable factorial structure of TILS in the Indian context.

The second study is based on a sample of 524 respondents. Again, Table 1 provides details of the sampling technique, size, method of data collection, and scales used, and Table-2 illustrates the sampling description. The Cronbach's alpha (CA) and composite reliability (CR) values of 0.754 and 0.824 (greater than 0.70) suggest the reliability of TILS in the Indian context. The Average Variance Extracted (AVE) estimate of 0.611 confirms the convergent validity of TILS for Indian respondents. The construct (convergent) validity was evaluated using two different scales of loneliness, i.e., the TILS scale and the revised UCLA loneliness scale. Table 4 reports a statistically significant positive association between two loneliness scores (r = 0.621, p < .01), which recommended the construct validity of TILS in the Indian context. To test the criterion validity of TILS in the Indian context, the correlation coefficients between TILS, GQ-6, and social connectedness were calculated. The broaden-and-build theory of positive emotions suggests that gratitude builds psychological and social resources like social

connections, trustworthy friends, social affiliation, and groups (Fredrickson, 2004). Thus, a person high on gratitude is less likely to feel lonely. Similarly, previous researchers like Trucharte et al. (2021) reported that people high in social connectedness were less likely to feel loneliness. Thus, a negative correlation was hypothesized between loneliness and gratitude & between loneliness and social connectedness. The correlation matrix illustrated in Table 4 revealed that TILS scores are negatively correlated with gratitude scores (r = − 0.410, p < .01) and the social connectedness scale (r = − 0.365, p < .01). These findings conclude the criterion validity of the TILS scale in Indian settings.

The present study's findings contribute to the existing literature and scientific knowledge of loneliness, which has not been studied and explored enough in Indian psychology. The generalization of the TILS in the Indian context is bound to encourage more studies on conceptualization, antecedents, and aftermaths of loneliness. Indian psychologists may use validated TILS to measure different stages of loneliness, and accordingly, appropriate interventions may be devised. The validated TILS scale could be used for early detection of loneliness, and subsequently, the associated psychological disorders could be arrested in the bud. It is also reported that gratitude is negatively related to loneliness. Thus, various gratitude interventions like gratitude journaling, gratitude letters, subsequent visits, introspection, meditation, mindfulness, etc., could be used to counter loneliness. Although the study offers interesting findings, there are limitations to the analysis. First, the study is based on convenience sampling, which has its own limitations. Future researchers may rely on a random sample to better generalise the results. Second, only internal consistency reliability is considered here. Finally, this is a cross-sectional study; thus, examining changes in loneliness through time could potentially identify those conditions enhancing and suppressing loneliness.
• The challenge of loneliness is poised to increase in the coming years.
• EFA and CFA recommend factorial validity of the three-item loneliness scale.
• The CA and CR values indicate the appropriate reliability of the scale in the Indian context. Also, other measures conclude the construct and criterion validity of the scale.
